headline: Tamotsu is 手 (ta, “hand”, bound apophonic form) plus 持つ (motsu, “to hold”).
Ha, “blade”, is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pa, and is cognate with 歯 (ha, “tooth”).
マイナス is from English minus.
Yubisasu is 指 (yubi, “finger”) plus 差す (sasu, “to extend”).
Saegiru is a shift from older さいぎる, itself from さきぎる (sakigiru), 先 (saki, “in front”) plus 切る (kiru, “cut”).
Kogitte is 小 (ko-, “little”) plus 切手 (kitte, “postage stamp”), with kitte voiced to gitte by rendaku.
Sodachi is the continuative stem of the verb 育つ (sodatsu, “to be raised, to grow up”).
ボルト covers “volt” and “bolt”, and the source borrows both from English.
Nafuda is 名 (na, “name”) plus 札 (fuda, “card, tag”).
ハンガー is borrowed from English hanger.
Myaku, “pulse”, is from Middle Chinese 脈 (MC meak).
Yoshi is the conclusive form of Classical Japanese adjective 良し (yoshi), modern 良い (yoi).
Tejō is 手 (te, “hand”) plus 錠 (jō, “lock”).
Ryōshin is 良 (ryō, “good”) plus 心 (shin, “heart”).
Hōshanō is 放射 (hōsha, “radiating, emitting”) plus 能 (nō, “ability, capacity”).
Hama is from Old Japanese and Proto-Japonic, and is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Hitome is 人 (hito, “person”) plus 目 (me, “eye”).
Oiru is from the Old Japanese verb 老ゆ (oyu).
Fukaketsu is from Middle Chinese 不可缺.
Awasete is the -te form of the verb 合わせる (awaseru, “to bring or put together”).
Ten, “heaven”, is from Middle Chinese 天 (MC then, “sky; heavens”).
ストロー is from English straw.
Futan is from Sinitic 負擔 (fùdān).
Bunshi is from Middle Chinese 分子 (pjun tsiX).
ユニーク is from English unique.
バッグ is borrowed from English bag.
Toriatsukau is 取る (toru) plus 扱う (atsukau).
ロマンチック is from English romantic.
Yohodo is likely a back-formation from 余っ程 (yoppodo), ultimately from よき (yoki, “good”) plus ほど (hodo, “extent”), with 余 an ateji.
Ninau is from classical 担ふ (ninafu), 荷 (ni, “load”) plus なふ (nafu, verb-forming suffix).
Kakumei is from Middle Chinese 革命 (“to switch to a new dynasty/regime”), and Fukuzawa Yukichi used it to translate English revolution.
